claim: Trisomy is deleterious and results in inviable or defective progeny if passed through the germ line.
source: Trisomy, the presence of a third copy of one chromosome, is deleterious and results in inviable or defective progeny if passed through the germ line.
evidence: This is a general statement about trisomy that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Random segregation of an extra chromosome is predicted to result in a high frequency of trisomic offspring from a trisomic parent.
source: Random segregation of an extra chromosome is predicted to result in a high frequency of trisomic offspring from a trisomic parent.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on Mendelian genetics principles.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans with trisomy of the X chromosome have far fewer trisomic offspring than expected.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans with trisomy of the X chromosome, however, have far fewer trisomic offspring than expected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations in the manuscript.

claim: The extra X chromosome was preferentially eliminated during anaphase I of female meiosis in C. elegans XXX worms.
source: We found that the extra X chromosome was preferentially eliminated during anaphase I of female meiosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Univalents lagged during anaphase I and their movement was biased toward the cortex and future polar body.
source: First, univalents lagged during anaphase I and their movement was biased toward the cortex and future polar body.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Late-lagging univalents were frequently captured by the ingressing polar body contractile ring.
source: Second, late-lagging univalents were frequently captured by the ingressing polar body contractile ring.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data.

claim: The asymmetry of female meiosis can partially correct pre-existing trisomy.
source: The asymmetry of female meiosis can thus partially correct pre-existing trisomy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: During female meiosis, a G2 oocyte containing four genome copies undergoes two asymmetric cell divisions depositing one genome in a single haploid egg, while the other three genomes are segregated into polar bodies.
source: During female meiosis, a G2 oocyte containing four genome copies undergoes two asymmetric cell divisions depositing one genome in a single haploid egg, while the other three genomes are segregated into polar bodies.
evidence: This describes the general process of female meiosis based on established knowledge.

claim: Meiotic spindles are asymmetrically positioned against the oocyte cortex with the pole-to-pole axis of the spindle perpendicular to the cortex.
source: These divisions are mediated by meiotic spindles that are asymmetrically positioned against the oocyte cortex with the pole-to-pole axis of the spindle perpendicular to the cortex.
evidence: This describes the characteristic positioning of meiotic spindles based on established knowledge.

claim: The inheritance of only one of the four genome copies and the distinct perpendicular positioning of the meiotic spindle are remarkably conserved among animal phyla.
source: Both the inheritance of only one of the four genome copies and the distinct perpendicular positioning of the meiotic spindle are remarkably conserved among animal phyla suggesting a selective advantage (Maro and Verlhac, 2002; Fabritius et al., 2011a; Maddox et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The conservation of asymmetric meiosis among animal phyla suggests a selective advantage.
source: Both the inheritance of only one of the four genome copies and the distinct perpendicular positioning of the meiotic spindle are remarkably conserved among animal phyla suggesting a selective advantage (Maro and Verlhac, 2002; Fabritius et al., 2011a; Maddox et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary principles and supported by citations.

claim: Asymmetric meiotic spindle positioning maximizes the volume of a single egg.
source: Asymmetric meiotic spindle positioning maximizes the volume of a single egg, helps prevent interference with the meiotic spindle by the sperm aster (McNally et al., 2012), and preserves predetermined embryonic polarity gradients.
evidence: This is a previously suggested advantage of asymmetric meiosis.

claim: Asymmetric meiotic spindle positioning helps prevent interference with the meiotic spindle by the sperm aster.
source: Asymmetric meiotic spindle positioning maximizes the volume of a single egg, helps prevent interference with the meiotic spindle by the sperm aster (McNally et al., 2012), and preserves predetermined embryonic polarity gradients.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Asymmetric meiotic spindle positioning preserves predetermined embryonic polarity gradients.
source: Asymmetric meiotic spindle positioning maximizes the volume of a single egg, helps prevent interference with the meiotic spindle by the sperm aster (McNally et al., 2012), and preserves predetermined embryonic polarity gradients.
evidence: This is a previously suggested advantage based on established knowledge.

claim: Asymmetric meiosis has the ability to correct trisomy by preferentially depositing the extra chromosome copy into a polar body.
source: Here, we suggest a previously unrecognized advantage of asymmetric meiosis, the ability of meiotic spindles to correct trisomy by preferentially depositing the extra chromosome copy into a polar body.
evidence: This is the novel hypothesis proposed and tested in this study.

claim: Accurate segregation of homologous chromosomes to opposite spindle poles depends on a physical attachment, or chiasma, between homologous chromosomes.
source: Accurate segregation of homologous chromosomes to opposite spindle poles depends on a physical attachment, or chiasma, between homologous chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chromosome segregation.

claim: A chiasma consists of a crossover, which holds the two homologous chromosomes together in a bivalent so that kinetochores can be properly oriented toward opposite poles.
source: A chiasma consists of a crossover, which holds the two homologous chromosomes together in a bivalent so that kinetochores can be properly oriented toward opposite poles (Moore and Orr-Weaver, 1998; Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When a chiasma does not form, univalent chromosomes may maintain sister cohesion and move to poles independent of their homologs at anaphase I as can occur in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: When a chiasma does not form, univalent chromosomes may maintain sister cohesion and move to poles independent of their homologs at anaphase I as can occur in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Buonomo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work in yeast.

claim: If a univalent chromosome biorients, loses cohesion, and segregates sister chromatids at anaphase I, the resulting single chromatid will segregate randomly at anaphase II.
source: If a univalent chromosome biorients, loses cohesion, and segregates sister chromatids at anaphase I (e.g., Nicklas and Jones, 1977; Lemaire-Adkins and Hunt, 2000; Kouznetsova et al., 2007), the resulting single chromatid will segregate randomly at anaphase II.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Random segregation of homologs at anaphase I or single chromatids at anaphase II should result in equal frequencies of haplo and diplo ova in the case of a trisomy.
source: Random segregation of homologs at anaphase I or single chromatids at anaphase II should result in equal frequencies of haplo and diplo ova in the case of a trisomy (Figure 1A) and equal frequencies of nullo and diplo ova in the case of a crossover failure.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on Mendelian genetics, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Random segregation should result in equal frequencies of nullo and diplo ova in the case of a crossover failure.
source: Random segregation of homologs at anaphase I or single chromatids at anaphase II should result in equal frequencies of haplo and diplo ova in the case of a trisomy (Figure 1A) and equal frequencies of nullo and diplo ova in the case of a crossover failure.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on Mendelian genetics.

claim: 100% of metaphase I meiotic embryos from XXX wild-type worms had 7 DAPI-staining bodies on the spindle.
source: We found that 100% of metaphase I meiotic embryos from XXX wild-type worms had 7 DAPI-staining bodies on the spindle (Figure 1C,F), consistent with 6 bivalents and a single univalent X.
evidence: This is a direct observation from fixed embryo imaging shown in Figure 1C,F.

claim: Two chromosomes were labeled with an X-specific FISH probe in metaphase I spindles from XXX wild-type worms.
source: Two chromosomes were labeled with an X-specific fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) probe in these spindles (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A mosaic gonad resulting from mitotic nondisjunction cannot explain the low frequency of XXX offspring from XXX worms.
source: This result shows that a mosaic gonad resulting from mitotic nondisjunction cannot explain the low frequency of XXX offspring from XXX worms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that all metaphase I spindles had 7 chromosomes.

claim: 71% of metaphase II spindles from XXX wild-type worms contained only 6 DAPI-staining bodies and only 29% contained 7 DAPI-staining bodies.
source: Instead, 71% of metaphase II spindles contained only 6 DAPI-staining bodies and only 29% contained 7 DAPI-staining bodies (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from fixed embryo imaging shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The frequencies of 71% 6-chromosome and 29% 7-chromosome metaphase II spindles match the 2:1 ratio of X to XX ova previously interpreted from genetic studies.
source: These frequencies match the 2:1 ratio of X to XX ova previously interpreted from genetic studies (Hodgkin et al., 1979) and are significantly different than the 50% expected from random segregation (one-tailed p = 0.004, Pearson's chi-squared test).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous genetic studies and statistical analysis.

claim: The metaphase II chromosome frequencies are significantly different than the 50% expected from random segregation (one-tailed p = 0.004).
source: These frequencies match the 2:1 ratio of X to XX ova previously interpreted from genetic studies (Hodgkin et al., 1979) and are significantly different than the 50% expected from random segregation (one-tailed p = 0.004, Pearson's chi-squared test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In 6/6 metaphase II embryos with only 6 DAPI-staining bodies, a single X hybridization signal was present in the spindle and 2–3 hybridization signals were present in the polar body.
source: FISH with an X-specific probe revealed that in 6/6 metaphase II embryos with only 6 DAPI-staining bodies, a single hybridization signal was present in the spindle and 2–3 hybridization signals were present in the polar body (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Only a single X-hybridization signal was observed in the first polar body in 5/5 spindles from diploids.
source: Because only a single X-hybridization signal was observed in the first polar body in 5/5 spindles from diploids, these results demonstrate that single X univalents are deposited in the first polar body with greater than 50% frequency.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments on diploid controls.

claim: Single X univalents are deposited in the first polar body with greater than 50% frequency.
source: Because only a single X-hybridization signal was observed in the first polar body in 5/5 spindles from diploids, these results demonstrate that single X univalents are deposited in the first polar body with greater than 50% frequency.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing XXX and diploid FISH results.

claim: Diakinesis stage him-8 oocytes have 5 autosomal bivalents and two X univalents.
source: It has previously been shown that diakinesis stage him-8 oocytes have 5 autosomal bivalents and two X univalents (Phillips et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: him-8 mutants produce a fivefold higher frequency of nulloX ova over diploX ova.
source: Instead, him-8 mutants produce a fivefold higher frequency of nulloX ova over diploX ova (Hodgkin et al., 1979), indicating that both maternal X univalents are lost at some time after diakinesis in a large fraction of embryos.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Both maternal X univalents are lost at some time after diakinesis in a large fraction of him-8 embryos.
source: Instead, him-8 mutants produce a fivefold higher frequency of nulloX ova over diploX ova (Hodgkin et al., 1979), indicating that both maternal X univalents are lost at some time after diakinesis in a large fraction of embryos.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic data cited.

claim: At meiosis I metaphase, 7 chromosomes were present in 96% of him-8 embryos.
source: At meiosis I metaphase, 7 chromosomes were present in 96% of him-8 embryos (Figure 2B,K), with the remainder having 6 chromosomes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from live and fixed embryo imaging shown in Figure 2B,K.

claim: 40% of him-8 metaphase II embryos had 5 chromosomes, 55% had 6 chromosomes, and only 5% had 7 chromosomes.
source: Instead, 40% of him-8 metaphase II embryos had 5 chromosomes, 55% had 6 chromosomes, and only 5% had 7 chromosomes (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a direct observation from live and fixed embryo imaging shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The metaphase II chromosome frequencies in him-8 differ significantly from those expected from unbiased segregation (chi-square test, two-tailed p < 0.0001).
source: These frequencies differ significantly from those expected from unbiased segregation (chi-square test, two-tailed p < 0.0001), closely match the ratio of nulloX to diploX ova inferred by Hodgkin et al. (1979) and support the hypothesis that the majority of X univalents are eliminated between metaphase I and metaphase II.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The metaphase II chromosome frequencies in him-8 closely match the ratio of nulloX to diploX ova inferred by Hodgkin et al. (1979).
source: These frequencies differ significantly from those expected from unbiased segregation (chi-square test, two-tailed p < 0.0001), closely match the ratio of nulloX to diploX ova inferred by Hodgkin et al. (1979) and support the hypothesis that the majority of X univalents are eliminated between metaphase I and metaphase II.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous genetic studies.

claim: The majority of X univalents are eliminated between metaphase I and metaphase II in him-8.
source: These frequencies differ significantly from those expected from unbiased segregation (chi-square test, two-tailed p < 0.0001), closely match the ratio of nulloX to diploX ova inferred by Hodgkin et al. (1979) and support the hypothesis that the majority of X univalents are eliminated between metaphase I and metaphase II.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chromosome count data.

claim: FISH revealed two X univalents and 7 total DAPI-staining bodies on 93% of all the him-8 metaphase I plates.
source: FISH revealed two X univalents and 7 total DAPI-staining bodies on 93% of all the him-8 metaphase I plates (Figure 2G,L).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 2G,L.

claim: When him-8 metaphase II spindles had 5 DAPI-staining bodies, at least two X hybridization foci were observed in the first polar body and none on the metaphase plate.
source: At metaphase II, FISH revealed at least two X hybridization foci in the first polar body and none on the metaphase plate when the spindle had 5 DAPI-staining bodies (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When him-8 metaphase II spindles had 6 DAPI-staining bodies, one X hybridization focus was observed on the metaphase plate and one in the first polar body.
source: When 6 DAPI-staining bodies were present on the metaphase II plate, we always observed one X hybridization focus each on the metaphase plate and in the first polar body (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 2I.

claim: When him-8 metaphase II spindles had 7 DAPI-staining bodies, two X hybridization foci were observed on the metaphase plate and none in the first polar body.
source: Finally, metaphase II embryos containing 7 DAPI-staining bodies had two X hybridization foci on the metaphase plate and none in the first polar body (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Both achiasmate X univalents are deposited into the first polar body in 40% of him-8 embryos as compared with the 25% expected from random segregation.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that both achiasmate X univalents are deposited into the first polar body in 40% of him-8 embryos as compared with the 25% expected from random segregation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the FISH data.

claim: Phillips and Dernburg reported only 72% of diakinesis oocytes with 7 rather than 6 DAPI-staining bodies in a zim-2 mutant.
source: Phillips and Dernburg reported only 72% of diakinesis oocytes with 7 rather than 6 DAPI-staining bodies in a zim-2 mutant, and our zim-2 strain with lacO(V) had only 62% of diakinesis oocytes with 7 DAPI-staining bodies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and confirmed by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: FISH revealed two distinct chromosome V hybridization foci and 7 DAPI-staining bodies on 41% of metaphase I spindles in zim-2.
source: FISH revealed two distinct chromosome V hybridization foci and 7 DAPI-staining bodies on 41% of metaphase I spindles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,E.

claim: 27% of zim-2 metaphase II embryos had five DAPI-staining bodies on the metaphase plate and chromosome V hybridization foci only in the first polar body.
source: Instead, FISH revealed 27% of metaphase II embryos had five DAPI-staining bodies on the metaphase plate and chromosome V hybridization foci only in the first polar body (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,E.

claim: Only 5% of zim-2 metaphase II spindles had 7 DAPI-staining bodies, two distinct chromosome V hybridization foci on the spindle, and none in the first polar body.
source: Likewise, random segregation of achiasmate V's should yield 10% metaphase II spindles with 7 DAPI-staining bodies on the metaphase II spindle, two distinct chromosome V hybridization foci on the spindle, and none in the first polar body. Only 5% of this embryo class was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The zim-2 metaphase II chromosome frequencies are significantly different than those expected from random segregation (chi-square test, two-tailed p < 0.0002).
source: These frequencies are significantly different than those expected from random segregation (chi-square test, two-tailed p < 0.0002).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Achiasmate autosomes, like achiasmate X chromosomes, are preferentially deposited into the first polar body.
source: Thus, achiasmate autosomes, like achiasmate X chromosomes, are preferentially deposited into the first polar body.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the zim-2 data.

claim: him-8 X univalents biorient at metaphase I.
source: The single REC-8 bands on wild-type metaphase II chromosomes and on him-8 metaphase I univalents were both oriented perpendicular to the pole-to-pole axis of the spindle (Figure 3D), indicating that him-8 X univalents biorient at metaphase I.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from REC-8 antibody staining shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of GFP::AIR-2 was 2.3 times higher on bivalents than univalents at metaphase I of him-8 embryos.
source: The fluorescence intensity of GFP::AIR-2 was 2.3 times higher on bivalents than univalents at metaphase I of him-8 embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: GFP::AIR-2 on metaphase II chromosomes was 1.7 times higher than on him-8 metaphase I univalents.
source: GFP::AIR-2 on metaphase II chromosomes was 1.7 times higher than on him-8 metaphase I univalents (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), indicating that the reduced amount of AIR-2 on metaphase I univalents was not simply a consequence of the smaller size of a univalent relative to a bivalent.
evidence: This is a direct observation from fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The reduced amount of AIR-2 on metaphase I univalents was not simply a consequence of the smaller size of a univalent relative to a bivalent.
source: GFP::AIR-2 on metaphase II chromosomes was 1.7 times higher than on him-8 metaphase I univalents (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), indicating that the reduced amount of AIR-2 on metaphase I univalents was not simply a consequence of the smaller size of a univalent relative to a bivalent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing AIR-2 levels on different chromosome types.

claim: him-8 univalents had 1.7 ± 0.3 times the intensity of REC-8 staining as the inter-homolog region of bivalents in the same spindle.
source: Consistent with the low levels of AIR-2, him-8 univalents had 1.7 ± 0.3 times the intensity of REC-8 staining as the inter-homolog region of bivalents in the same spindle (Figure 3B; n = 8 embryos, two-tailed p = 0.04, chi square relative to expected 1.0).
evidence: This is a direct observation from REC-8 antibody staining intensity measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 90% of him-8 embryos at anaphase I had one or two lagging chromosomes (n = 119) compared to 2% of wild-type embryos (n = 52).
source: 90% of him-8 embryos at anaphase I had one or two lagging chromosomes (n = 119) compared to 2% of wild-type embryos (n = 52) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In 51% of living him-8 embryos with lagging chromosomes at anaphase I, two discrete lagging chromosomes could be resolved.
source: In 51% of living him-8 embryos with lagging chromosomes at anaphase I, two discrete lagging chromosomes could be resolved.
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Each lagging chromosome eventually moved as a single unit either toward the cortex or into the embryo in 98% of him-8 embryos (n = 179).
source: Each lagging chromosome eventually moved as a single unit either toward the cortex or into the embryo in 98% of embryos (n = 179) (Figures 4B, 5A), indicating that cohesion between sister chromatids is maintained and that univalents are not broken or destroyed during anaphase.
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figures 4B and 5A.

claim: Cohesion between sister chromatids is maintained in lagging chromosomes and univalents are not broken or destroyed during anaphase.
source: Each lagging chromosome eventually moved as a single unit either toward the cortex or into the embryo in 98% of embryos (n = 179) (Figures 4B, 5A), indicating that cohesion between sister chromatids is maintained and that univalents are not broken or destroyed during anaphase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that lagging chromosomes move as single units.

claim: At anaphase II, only 10% of him-8 embryos exhibited lagging chromosomes (n = 60) and 0/22 wild-type embryos had lagging chromosomes.
source: At anaphase II, only 10% of him-8 embryos exhibited lagging chromosomes (n = 60) and 0/22 wild-type embryos had lagging chromosomes, suggesting that lagging chromosomes are caused by the presence of univalents at meiosis I.
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Lagging chromosomes are caused by the presence of univalents at meiosis I.
source: At anaphase II, only 10% of him-8 embryos exhibited lagging chromosomes (n = 60) and 0/22 wild-type embryos had lagging chromosomes, suggesting that lagging chromosomes are caused by the presence of univalents at meiosis I.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing anaphase I and II lagging frequencies.

claim: The X-specific FISH probe labeled one or two lagging chromosomes at anaphase I of him-8 embryos in 13/14 cases.
source: We found that the X-specific FISH probe labeled one or two lagging chromosomes at anaphase I of him-8 embryos, indicating that lagging chromosomes are X univalents (13/14) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Lagging chromosomes at anaphase I in him-8 are X univalents.
source: We found that the X-specific FISH probe labeled one or two lagging chromosomes at anaphase I of him-8 embryos, indicating that lagging chromosomes are X univalents (13/14) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from FISH labeling of lagging chromosomes.

claim: 36% of fixed him-8 anaphase I embryos with lagging chromosomes had two distinct FISH-positive chromosomes lagging.
source: 36% of fixed him-8 anaphase I embryos with lagging chromosomes had two distinct FISH-positive chromosomes lagging.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments.

claim: One or both X univalents lag in up to 90% of him-8 embryos.
source: These results suggest that one or both X univalents lag in up to 90% of him-8 embryos.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the FISH data on lagging chromosomes.

claim: 27% of zim-2 anaphase I spindles (4/15 or over half of anaphase I spindles expected to have V univalents) had a lagging chromosome.
source: Similar results were obtained for chromosome V in zim-2 mutants, where 40% of metaphase I embryos have univalent V's (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). 27% (4/15 or over half of anaphase I spindles expected to have V univalents) had a lagging chromosome.
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging zim-2 embryos.

claim: 100% (4/4) of lagging chromosomes in zim-2 were chromosome V as assayed by LacO(V) FISH.
source: 100% (4/4) of these lagging chromosomes were chromosome V as assayed by LacO(V) FISH (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Achiasmate autosomes lag at anaphase I, just like achiasmate X chromosomes.
source: These results indicate that achiasmate autosomes lag at anaphase I, just like achiasmate X chromosomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the zim-2 data.

claim: 65% of lagging chromosomes eventually moved toward the cortex and the forming polar body of him-8 embryos during anaphase I (n = 181).
source: Our time-lapse analysis revealed that 65% of lagging chromosomes eventually moved toward the cortex and the forming polar body of him-8 embryos during anaphase I (n = 181) (Figure 5B), indicating that preferential expulsion of lagging univalents into the first polar body could contribute to the higher than random frequency of metaphase II spindles with 5 autosomes and no X.
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Preferential expulsion of lagging univalents into the first polar body could contribute to the higher than random frequency of metaphase II spindles with 5 autosomes and no X.
source: Our time-lapse analysis revealed that 65% of lagging chromosomes eventually moved toward the cortex and the forming polar body of him-8 embryos during anaphase I (n = 181) (Figure 5B), indicating that preferential expulsion of lagging univalents into the first polar body could contribute to the higher than random frequency of metaphase II spindles with 5 autosomes and no X.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-lapse data.

claim: In wild type, ingression of the polar body contractile ring initiates when homologs have separated by 2.3 μm and polar body scission completes when homologs have separated by 5.6 μm.
source: In wild type, ingression of the polar body contractile ring initiates when homologs have separated by 2.3 μm and polar body scission completes when homologs have separated by 5.6 μm (Fabritius et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Early-resolving univalents moved toward the cortex 64% of the time (n = 72).
source: These were resolved toward the cortex 64% of the time (n = 72), and NMY-2 depletion had no significant effect on this class of embryos (p = 0.8) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NMY-2 depletion had no significant effect on early-resolving univalents (p = 0.8).
source: These were resolved toward the cortex 64% of the time (n = 72), and NMY-2 depletion had no significant effect on this class of embryos (p = 0.8) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RNAi depletion of NMY-2 in him-8 embryos resulted in a significant (p = 0.02) reduction in the percentage of late-lagging univalents resolving toward the cortex from 64% to 43%.
source: Indeed, RNAi depletion of the non-muscle myosin, NMY-2, which causes complete loss of cortical furrowing and polar body formation (Fabritius et al., 2011b), in him-8 embryos resulted in a significant (p = 0.02) reduction in the percentage of late-lagging univalents resolving toward the cortex from 64% to 43% (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: mel-11 increased the segregation bias of him-8 by sevenfold from 3:1 to 23:1.
source: We found that mel-11 increased the segregation bias of him-8 by sevenfold from 3:1 to 23:1 (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from genetic crosses shown in Table 1.

claim: More rapid furrow ingression captures more lagging univalents in the first polar body resulting in more nulloX ova.
source: This result indicates that more rapid furrow ingression captures more lagging univalents in the first polar body resulting in more nulloX ova.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mel-11 genetic data.

claim: In him-8 embryos, when there were no lagging univalents, the contractile ring ingressed normally to 50% spindle length as measured from the outside edge of the main chromatin mass in the interior of the embryo.
source: In him-8 embryos, when there were no lagging univalents, the contractile ring ingressed normally to 50% spindle length as measured from the outside edge of the main chromatin mass in the interior of the embryo.
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: When a lagging univalent was seen segregating into the embryo, the contractile ring ingressed inward to a shallower depth at 59% spindle length.
source: Alternatively, when a lagging univalent was seen segregating into the embryo, the contractile ring ingressed inward to a shallower depth at 59% spindle length (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: In 5/10 him-8 embryos in which the septin-labeled ring reached the lagging univalent, the univalent was trapped in the septin tube and moved with the septin tube outward during cortical relaxation.
source: In 5/10 him-8 embryos in which the septin-labeled ring reached the lagging univalent, the univalent was trapped in the septin tube and moved with the septin tube outward during cortical relaxation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In 3/10 cases, the septin ring passed the univalent before the tube was formed, and in these cases, the univalent joined the main mass of chromatin in the polar body.
source: In 3/10 cases, the septin ring passed the univalent before the tube was formed, and in these cases, the univalent joined the main mass of chromatin in the polar body.
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: In 2/10 cases where the univalent did not end up in the polar body, the univalent slipped out of the septin tube into the embryo before the septin tube moved toward the embryo surface.
source: In the 2/10 cases where the univalent did not end up in the polar body, the univalent slipped out of the septin tube into the embryo before the septin tube moved toward the embryo surface.
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: The septin tube traps late-lagging univalents until scission occurs on the embryo side of the septin tube.
source: These results are consistent with a model where the septin tube traps late-lagging univalents until scission occurs on the embryo side of the septin tube.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the septin imaging data.

claim: RNAi of ANI-3 initiated on L4 him-8 hermaphrodites significantly (p < 0.001 binomial test) reduced the fraction of XO male progeny from 37% (n = 9 mothers, 1960 progeny) to 27% (n = 11 mothers, 2123 progeny).
source: Indeed, RNAi of ANI-3 initiated on L4 him-8 hermaphrodites (which have already completed spermatogenesis) significantly (p < 0.001 binomial test) reduced the fraction of XO male progeny from 37% (n = 9 mothers, 1960 progeny) to 27% (n = 11 mothers, 2123 progeny), whereas ani-3 (RNAi) had no significant effect on wild-type worms (wt: 0.04% XO, 1% dead, n = 11 mothers; ani-3 [RNAi]: 0.05% XO, 1% dead, n = 17 mothers).
evidence: This is a direct observation from RNAi experiments.

claim: ani-3 (RNAi) had no significant effect on wild-type worms.
source: Indeed, RNAi of ANI-3 initiated on L4 him-8 hermaphrodites (which have already completed spermatogenesis) significantly (p < 0.001 binomial test) reduced the fraction of XO male progeny from 37% (n = 9 mothers, 1960 progeny) to 27% (n = 11 mothers, 2123 progeny), whereas ani-3 (RNAi) had no significant effect on wild-type worms (wt: 0.04% XO, 1% dead, n = 11 mothers; ani-3 [RNAi]: 0.05% XO, 1% dead, n = 17 mothers).
evidence: This is a direct observation from RNAi experiments.

claim: Compromising the integrity of the septin tube may reduce the efficiency of trapping lagging univalents in the septin tube.
source: This result suggests that compromising the integrity of the septin tube may reduce the efficiency of trapping lagging univalents in the septin tube.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ANI-3 RNAi results.

claim: ANI-3 depletion did not significantly increase the frequency of XXX dumpy progeny from him-8 mothers (him-8: 3% XXX, 5% dead; him-8 ani-3[RNAi]: 4% XXX, 6% dead).
source: ANI-3 depletion did not significantly increase the frequency of XXX dumpy progeny from him-8 mothers (him-8: 3% XXX, 5% dead; him-8 ani-3[RNAi]: 4% XXX, 6% dead).
evidence: This is a direct observation from RNAi experiments.

claim: Univalents were misaligned toward the spindle poles in fixed him-8 embryos at late metaphase I, when the meiotic spindle is shortened but not yet rotated.
source: We found that univalents were misaligned toward the spindle poles in fixed him-8 embryos at late metaphase I, when the meiotic spindle is shortened but not yet rotated (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from fixed embryo imaging shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: In 46% of late metaphase I him-8 embryos, both univalents were misaligned toward the same pole.
source: In 46% of these embryos, both univalents were misaligned toward the same pole (Figure 7B), close to the 50% expected from random positioning.
evidence: This is a direct observation from fixed embryo imaging shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In fixed him-8 embryos at the onset of anaphase, when spindles are shortened and rotated but chromosomes are not yet separated, 57% had one or both univalents closer to the cortical pole (38 + 19%).
source: In fixed him-8 embryos at the onset of anaphase, when spindles are shortened and rotated but chromosomes are not yet separated, 57% had one or both univalents closer to the cortical pole (38 + 19%; Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from fixed embryo imaging shown in Figure 7F,G.

claim: No him-8 embryos at the onset of anaphase had both univalents closer to the interior spindle pole.
source: No embryos had both univalents closer to the interior spindle pole.
evidence: This is a direct observation from fixed embryo imaging.

claim: At 20°C, the mei-2(ct98) him-8 double mutant produced only 21% male progeny (n = 1440 progeny from 14 parents), which is significantly less than the 36% male progeny produced by the him-8 single mutant (n = 964 progeny from 8 parents; p < 0.0001 by one-tailed binomial test).
source: At 20°C, the mei-2(ct98) him-8 double mutant produced only 21% male progeny (n = 1440 progeny from 14 parents), which is significantly less than the 36% male progeny produced by the him-8 single mutant (n = 964 progeny from 8 parents; p < 0.0001 by one-tailed binomial test) and is significantly different than mei-2 (ct98) alone (0% males; n = 925 progeny from 8 parents).
evidence: This is a direct observation from genetic crosses.

claim: The mei-2(ct98) him-8 double mutant male progeny frequency is significantly different than mei-2 (ct98) alone (0% males; n = 925 progeny from 8 parents).
source: At 20°C, the mei-2(ct98) him-8 double mutant produced only 21% male progeny (n = 1440 progeny from 14 parents), which is significantly less than the 36% male progeny produced by the him-8 single mutant (n = 964 progeny from 8 parents; p < 0.0001 by one-tailed binomial test) and is significantly different than mei-2 (ct98) alone (0% males; n = 925 progeny from 8 parents).
evidence: This is a direct observation from genetic crosses.

claim: In 6/8 particularly clear time-lapse sequences where one or both univalents could be identified unambiguously 10–100 s before initiation of spindle rotation, the univalent-proximal pole rotated to the cortex.
source: In 8 particularly clear time-lapse sequences, one or both univalents could be identified unambiguously 10–100 s before initiation of spindle rotation. In 6/8 of these cases, the univalent-proximal pole rotated to the cortex (Figure 7I,H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 7I,H.

claim: Among 30 embryos in which one or two lagging chromosomes were already positioned closer to one pole at anaphase I onset and the lagging chromosome resolved early, the lagging chromosome resolved toward the pole that it was already close to in 80% of these embryos.
source: Time-lapse imaging of spindles after rotation revealed that among 30 embryos in which one or two lagging chromosomes were already positioned closer to one pole at anaphase I onset and the lagging chromosome resolved early, the lagging chromosome resolved toward the pole that it was already close to in 80% of these embryos (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: The observations are not consistent with a cortical pole that generates a stronger pulling force after rotation but instead favor the idea that the offset position of univalents before rotation increases the probability that the univalent-proximal pole will move to the cortex.
source: These observations are not consistent with a cortical pole that generates a stronger pulling force after rotation but instead favor the idea that the offset position of univalents before rotation increases the probability that the univalent-proximal pole will move to the cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Before pronuclear meeting, male pronuclei are distinguished from female pronuclei by the presence of sperm asters.
source: Before pronuclear meeting, male pronuclei are distinguished from female pronuclei by the presence of sperm asters.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans embryology.

claim: 90% haploX, 8% nulloX, and 2% diploX male pronuclei were observed in self-fertilized him-8 mothers (n = 52).
source: We observed 90% haploX, 8% nulloX, and 2% diploX male pronuclei (n = 52).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH on pronuclear stage embryos.

claim: The male pronuclei frequencies are significantly different than the 50%, 25%, 25% expected from random segregation (two-tailed p < 0.0001 by chi square).
source: These values are significantly different than the 50%, 25%, 25% expected from random segregation (two-tailed p < 0.0001 by chi square) and are similar to the frequencies obtained by Hodgkin et al. (1979) using genetic tests with sex-reversed him-8 XX males.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The male pronuclei frequencies are similar to the frequencies obtained by Hodgkin et al. (1979) using genetic tests with sex-reversed him-8 XX males.
source: These values are significantly different than the 50%, 25%, 25% expected from random segregation (two-tailed p < 0.0001 by chi square) and are similar to the frequencies obtained by Hodgkin et al. (1979) using genetic tests with sex-reversed him-8 XX males.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous genetic studies.

claim: 10% nulloX sperm make a small contribution to reducing the frequency of XXX self-progeny.
source: 10% nulloX sperm thus make a small contribution to reducing the frequency of XXX self-progeny.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pronuclear FISH data.

claim: Women with trisomy 21 or trisomy X are often fertile and have been reported to have more than 50% euploid offspring.
source: However, women with trisomy 21 or trisomy X are often fertile and have been reported to have more than 50% euploid offspring (Bovicelli et al., 1982; Neri, 1984; Ratcliffe et al., 1991; Robinson et al., 1991; Stewart et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Eggs produced by triploid oyster females and fertilized with sperm from diploid males result in 57% diploid, 31% triploid, and 12% aneuploid offspring.
source: Eggs produced by triploid females and fertilized with sperm from diploid males result in 57% diploid, 31% triploid, and 12% aneuploid offspring, whereas eggs produced by diploids and fertilized by sperm from triploids result in 15% diploid and 85% aneuploid offspring (Gong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on oysters.

claim: Eggs produced by diploid oysters and fertilized by sperm from triploids result in 15% diploid and 85% aneuploid offspring.
source: Eggs produced by triploid females and fertilized with sperm from diploid males result in 57% diploid, 31% triploid, and 12% aneuploid offspring, whereas eggs produced by diploids and fertilized by sperm from triploids result in 15% diploid and 85% aneuploid offspring (Gong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on oysters.

claim: Triploid oysters and trisomic human oocytes sometimes form trivalent structures rather than a separate bivalent and univalent.
source: In contrast with trisomic C. elegans, triploid oysters (Guo and Allen, 1994) and trisomic human oocytes sometimes form trivalent structures rather than a separate bivalent and univalent.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only 42–16% of diplotene oocytes from fetuses with trisomy 21, trisomy 13, or trisomy 18 exhibited a separate bivalent and univalent.
source: Only 42–16% of diplotene oocytes from fetuses with trisomy 21, trisomy 13, or trisomy 18 exhibited a separate bivalent and univalent (Roig et al., 2005; Robles et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the 44–78% of oocytes from XO mice in which the univalent segregates intact at anaphase I, the univalent is preferentially retained in the embryo.
source: In the 44–78% of oocytes from XO mice in which the univalent segregates intact at anaphase I, the univalent is preferentially retained in the embryo (Lemaire-Adkins and Hunt, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on mice.

claim: Sex-reversed XO C. elegans produce an excess of nulloX ova.
source: This appears to be a difference between worms and mice rather than a difference between a trisomy and a monosomy since sex-reversed XO C. elegans produce an excess of nulloX ova (Hodgkin, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The efficiency of placing univalents in the first polar body has evolved to a point that corrects trisomy without reducing the frequency of haploid eggs produced from oocytes that failed to form a chiasma between one pair of homologs.
source: Thus, the efficiency of placing univalents in the first polar body has evolved to a point that corrects trisomy without reducing the frequency of haploid eggs produced from oocytes that failed to form a chiasma between one pair of homologs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing no significant decrease in haploid eggs.
